title: 42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
content:
A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.”
42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
A bipartisan coalition of AGs say Character.AI is planning to sell the personal data of minors to the highest bidder.
In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs.
The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed.
Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

report.summary: Forty-two state attorneys general are opposing Character.AI's bankruptcy plan to sell chat histories, including data from millions of minors, without user safeguards.
report.background: Character.AI's bankruptcy follows years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. In October, the company filed for Chapter 11; Disney then bought some assets and hired CEO Karandeep Anand and several technical staff, an acquihire-style deal that also drew broad AG opposition. The dispute sits at the intersection of bankruptcy law and AI privacy: companion chatbots encourage intimate, long-running conversations, creating valuable data assets. When an AI company fails, users' chats can become saleable assets unless contracts, privacy policies, or regulators block it. States are increasingly passing chatbot and minors' safety laws, and the AG coalition argues that a bankruptcy sale should not erase privacy commitments. The case could set a precedent for how AI firms handle sensitive conversation logs during distress.
key_points: A bipartisan group of 42 state attorneys general wants to stop Character.AI from auctioning private chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts. About 2.1 million of those accounts belong to minors, according to the AGs, and they say the sale plan includes no protections for the people whose conversations would change hands.

Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in October after years of scandals and legal fights. Disney bought some assets and hired CEO Karandeep Anand plus several technical staff in an acquihire-style deal. A similarly broad AG coalition opposed that Disney transaction, signaling sustained state scrutiny of Character.AI's data and corporate maneuvers.

The AGs say the sale lacks basic safeguards: buyers would not be required to honor existing privacy policies, users would have no clear way to delete their data, and nothing would stop a buyer from reselling the chats to another party. That combination turns sensitive personal conversations into an open-ended commercial asset.

The first bidder has almost no public track record. It was established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed, according to the article. The AGs argue that such a thin paper trail makes it harder to hold the buyer accountable or trust promises about data handling.

New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado have passed chatbot-related laws that take effect January 1st, 2027. Character.AI may be in violation of those rules when they start, adding another layer of legal risk beyond the bankruptcy sale and the AG opposition.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case is a warning that privacy policies and user trust can become bargaining chips in bankruptcy. Companion-app makers may face pressure to minimize chat retention, offer deletion and export, and clarify what happens to data in insolvency. Developers should treat conversation logs as sensitive personal data, not free training or sale inventory, and build consent, retention limits, and self-hosting options. For regular users, the lesson is blunt: intimate chats with AI may not stay private if the company fails or sells assets. Users should avoid sharing sensitive details, check deletion tools, and consider local or privacy-focused alternatives, especially for minors.
report.tools: To follow up, watch open-source, self-hosted chat stacks such as Ollama with Open WebUI, LibreChat, and llama.cpp for running models locally so conversations stay on your device. Privacy Guides and the EFF offer practical data-privacy guidance; state AG filings and court dockets track the Character.AI bankruptcy. For developers, review data-retention, deletion, and consent patterns before shipping companion chatbots.
